title: Chapter 1: Matter and Measurement — ASC0304 Chemistry I

questions.q:
A sample of matter is analysed and found to consist of only one type of atom bonded together in a fixed 1:1 ratio, and it cannot be separated into simpler substances by physical means alone. Which of the following best classifies this sample?

A. Element

B. Homogeneous mixture

C. Compound

D. Heterogeneous mixture
questions.answer:
Correct answer: C

A substance made of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, which cannot be separated by physical methods, is a compound (physical separation only works on mixtures).

questions.q:
Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture?

A. Granite rock

B. Brass (a solid alloy of copper and zinc)

C. Gravel

D. Whole milk
questions.answer:
Correct answer: B

Brass is a solid solution (alloy) — its composition is uniform throughout, so it is homogeneous. Granite, gravel, and whole milk all show visibly distinguishable components (heterogeneous).

questions.q:
Which of the following is an example of a chemical change?

A. Milk turning sour over time

B. Ice melting into liquid water

C. Sugar dissolving in hot tea

D. Mercury vaporising at room temperature
questions.answer:
Correct answer: A

Souring of milk produces new substances (e.g. lactic acid) via a chemical reaction. The other three options only change the state or dispersion of the substance — the chemical composition is unchanged.

questions.q:
How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.020070 km?

A. 3

B. 4

C. 6

D. 5
questions.answer:
Correct answer: D

Leading zeros (0.0) are not significant; the digits 2, 0, 0, 7, 0 are all significant (captive zeros and a trailing zero after the decimal point) — 5 significant figures.

questions.q:
The number 0.0004070 is correctly expressed in scientific notation as:

A. 4.07 × 10⁻⁴

B. 4.070 × 10⁻⁴

C. 40.70 × 10⁻⁵

D. 4.070 × 10⁻³
questions.answer:
Correct answer: B

The coefficient must lie between 1 and 10 (rules out option C), and all 4 significant figures of the original number (4, 0, 7, 0) must be preserved with exponent −4.

questions.q:
A liquid flows through a tube at a rate of 45 mL/min. What is this flow rate in L/hr?

A. 0.75 L/hr

B. 27.0 L/hr

C. 0.027 L/hr

D. 2.70 L/hr
questions.answer:
Correct answer: D

Converting mL/min to L/hr using dimensional analysis:

45 mL/min × 60 min/hr × (1 L)/(1000 mL) = 2.70 L/hr

questions.q:
Which of the following quantities is an exact number, with an infinite number of significant figures?

A. The conversion factor 1000 mL = 1 L

B. A measured mass of 5.02 g

C. A measured temperature of 25.3 °C

D. The number of moles calculated from a measured mass
questions.answer:
Correct answer: A

A defined conversion factor (1000 mL = 1 L, by definition) is exact. Measured quantities, and any value calculated from them, always carry a limited, finite number of significant figures.

questions.q:
A student titrates a solution three times and obtains 24.98 mL, 24.95 mL and 25.01 mL. The accepted (theoretical) value is 25.00 mL. Which statement best describes this data set?

A. High accuracy, low precision

B. Low accuracy, high precision

C. High accuracy, high precision

D. Low accuracy, low precision

SECTION B: Structured / Subjective Questions
questions.answer:
Correct answer: C

All three readings (24.98, 24.95, 25.01 mL) are very close to the accepted value of 25.00 mL (high accuracy) and very close to each other, within 0.06 mL of one another (high precision).

Section B: Structured / Subjective Questions

questions.q:
Classify each of the following substances as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture. Give one reason for each answer.

(a) Aluminium foil

(b) Sparkling mineral water (a solution of dissolved carbon dioxide gas in water)

(c) Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide, CO2)

(d) Pewter (a solid alloy of tin and lead)
questions.answer:
(a) Aluminium foil — element. Made of only one type of atom (Al); cannot be broken down further by chemical means.

(b) Sparkling mineral water — homogeneous mixture. CO2 gas and water (plus dissolved minerals) are physically mixed with uniform composition throughout; components are not visible.

(c) Dry ice (solid CO2) — compound. Two elements (C and O) chemically bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio; can only be broken down by a chemical reaction.

(d) Pewter — homogeneous mixture (alloy). Two elements (Sn and Pb) physically combined in variable proportion with a uniform appearance.

questions.q: Nitrogen gas, N₂, and ammonia gas, NH₃, are both molecules. Explain why N₂ is classified as an element while NH₃ is classified as a compound, even though both exist as discrete molecules.
questions.answer:
N2 is built from only one type of atom (nitrogen). Although it is a molecule (two atoms bonded together), it contains a single element, so it is classified as an element.

NH3 contains two different types of atoms (nitrogen and hydrogen) chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, so it is classified as a compound.

Conclusion: classification as element vs compound depends on the number of different types of atoms present, not on whether the substance exists as a molecule — every compound is a molecule/formula unit, but not every molecule is a compound.

questions.q:
Classify each of the following as a homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture, giving a reason.

(a) Fog (tiny water droplets suspended in air)

(b) Muddy river water

(c) Liquefied petroleum gas, LPG (a mixture of propane and butane gases)

(d) A vinaigrette salad dressing that separates into an oil layer and a vinegar layer
questions.answer:
(a) Fog — heterogeneous. Suspended water droplets are physically distinguishable from the surrounding air; composition is not uniform at all points.

(b) Muddy river water — heterogeneous. Suspended soil particles are visibly distinguishable from the water and will settle out.

(c) LPG (propane + butane) — homogeneous. Two gases mixed uniformly at the molecular level with no visible boundary.

(d) Vinaigrette dressing — heterogeneous. Two distinct, visible layers (oil and vinegar) exist, so composition differs from one part of the sample to another.

questions.q: A student claims: "Sugar water is a compound, because the sugar chemically combines with the water." Evaluate this statement. Is it correct? Give two reasons to support your answer.
questions.answer:
The statement is incorrect. Sugar water is a homogeneous mixture (solution), not a compound.

Reason 1: The sugar dissolves in water without any chemical reaction — no new substance is formed; the sugar and water molecules keep their own chemical identities.

Reason 2: Sugar water has a variable composition (it can be made more or less concentrated), whereas a compound always has a fixed composition. Sugar water can also be separated back into sugar and water by a physical method (e.g. evaporation), whereas a compound cannot be separated by physical means.

questions.q:
Classify each of the following changes as a physical or chemical change, with a brief justification.

(a) Iodine crystals subliming directly into purple vapour

(b) A silver spoon slowly tarnishing (turning black) on exposure to air

(c) Tearing a sheet of paper into small pieces

(d) Digesting a slice of bread in the stomach
questions.answer:
(a) Physical change — sublimation is only a change of state (solid to gas); the I2 molecules themselves are unchanged.

(b) Chemical change — tarnishing forms a new substance, silver sulfide (Ag2S), through reaction with sulfur compounds in the air.

(c) Physical change — the paper's shape and size change, but its chemical composition (cellulose) is unchanged.

(d) Chemical change — digestion breaks large molecules down into new, simpler substances through chemical reactions.

questions.q: Using ethanol as an example, explain why boiling point is classified as a physical property while flammability is classified as a chemical property.
questions.answer:
Boiling point is a physical property: when ethanol boils, only its physical state changes from liquid to gas — the C2H5OH molecules themselves are not altered, so no new substance is formed.

Flammability is a chemical property: it describes ethanol's ability to undergo a chemical reaction (combustion with oxygen) that produces entirely new substances (CO2 and H2O) with a different chemical composition from the starting ethanol.

questions.q: A measurement is reported simply as "25". Explain why this is meaningless in chemistry, using the two possible readings 25 mL and 25 g as an example.
questions.answer:
A measurement must always contain both a number (quantitative part) and a unit (qualitative part) to have meaning. The number 25 alone does not tell us what physical quantity was measured.

25 mL describes a volume, while 25 g describes a mass — completely different physical quantities. Without the unit attached, the number 25 conveys no useful chemical information.

questions.q: Give two reasons why the SI (International System of Units) is preferred over the Imperial system for scientific work in chemistry.
questions.answer:
Reason 1: SI units are based on consistent powers of 10 (via metric prefixes), making conversions between unit sizes (e.g. g to kg) simple multiplication/division, unlike Imperial units which use irregular conversion factors (e.g. 12 inches = 1 foot).

Reason 2: SI is a single, internationally agreed standard used globally in science, industry and commerce, avoiding confusion when scientists from different countries share and compare data.

questions.q:
State the SI base unit and its symbol for each of the following quantities:

(a) Amount of substance

(b) Thermodynamic temperature

(c) Electric current

(d) Time
questions.answer:
(a) Amount of substance — mole (mol)

(b) Thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K)

(c) Electric current — ampere (A)

(d) Time — second (s)

questions.q: Density is a derived quantity, not an SI base quantity. Starting from the definition density = mass ÷ volume, show how the derived SI unit of density, kg m⁻³, is obtained from the SI base units of mass and length.
questions.answer:
density = mass/volume

The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). The SI base unit of length is the metre (m), so volume (length × length × length) has SI unit m3:

volume unit = m × m × m = m³

Substituting the units of mass and volume into the density expression:

density unit = kg/m³

A quantity divided by a cubed unit is equivalent to that quantity multiplied by the unit raised to the power −3, so:

density unit = kg m⁻³

questions.q: A student records a burette reading as 12.50 mL, while another records it as 12.5 mL for what should be the same reading. Explain, in terms of implied precision, why these two records are not equivalent.
questions.answer:
12.50 mL has 4 significant figures — it implies the volume was estimated to the nearest 0.01 mL (the hundredths digit is the uncertain, estimated digit).

12.5 mL has only 3 significant figures — it implies the volume was only estimated to the nearest 0.1 mL. Dropping the trailing zero falsely suggests the measurement is ten times less precise than it actually was.

questions.q: Explain why a pipette or volumetric flask is a more precise instrument for delivering exactly 25.00 mL of solution than a graduated cylinder, in terms of how each instrument is calibrated.
questions.answer:
A pipette/volumetric flask has a single calibration mark etched onto the glass and is manufactured to deliver or contain exactly one specific volume with very high precision, so the uncertainty in the last digit is extremely small (e.g. ±0.02 mL).

A graduated cylinder has multiple graduations spaced further apart, so the observer must estimate the last digit between two marks, giving a larger uncertainty (e.g. ±0.1 to ±1 mL). It is therefore lower-precision than a pipette for delivering one fixed volume.

questions.q: A student reads a thermometer as 36.6 °C. Explain why the final digit, 6, must always be an estimate rather than a digit read with certainty.
questions.answer:
No measuring instrument has infinitely fine graduations. The certain digits can be read directly from the marked graduations (e.g. the 36 °C mark), but the position between the smallest graduation marks must be judged by eye.

This last digit (the tenths digit, 6) is therefore always an estimate — the one uncertain digit that is still recorded because it carries useful information about the true value.

questions.q: Distinguish between accuracy and precision in a chemistry experiment. Your answer should refer to what each term is compared against.
questions.answer:
Accuracy describes how close a measured (experimental) value is to the true or accepted (theoretical) value — it is assessed by calculating percentage error.

Precision describes how close a set of repeated measurements are to one another (their reproducibility), regardless of whether they are close to the true value — it does not require knowledge of the theoretical value at all.

questions.q: Explain, with an example scenario, how a set of experimental data can be precise but not accurate.
questions.answer:
This occurs when there is a systematic error (e.g. a miscalibrated balance that always reads 0.50 g too high) affecting every measurement in the same way.

Example: a poorly zeroed balance gives readings of 50.52 g, 50.50 g, 50.51 g for repeated weighings of the same object. These values are very close to each other (high precision, small spread), but if the object's true mass is 50.00 g, every reading is off by about 0.50 g, so the data is not accurate (high percentage error) despite being precise.

questions.q:
For each of the following, state whether it is an exact number or a measured number, and give a reason.

(a) 12 test tubes counted on a rack

(b) A mass of 15.6 g read from a digital balance

(c) The defined relationship 1 dozen = 12

(d) The conversion factor 1 atm = 760 mmHg
questions.answer:
(a) Exact number — obtained by counting whole, discrete objects, so there is no uncertainty in it.

(b) Measured number — comes from reading an instrument (a balance), so it carries an estimated last digit and a limited number of significant figures.

(c) Exact number — a defined relationship (by definition, not by measurement), so it has infinite significant figures.

(d) Exact number — a defined conversion factor between two pressure units, so it does not limit the number of significant figures in a calculation.

questions.q: Explain why the zero in 0.0250 g is not significant, while the zero in 2.05 g is significant.
questions.answer:
In 0.0250 g, the first zero (before the 2) is a leading zero — leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are never significant.

In 2.05 g, the zero lies between two non-zero digits (2 and 5) — it is a captive zero, and captive zeros are always significant.

questions.q: The number 4500 g (written with no decimal point) is ambiguous in terms of significant figures. Explain the ambiguity, and explain how writing the number in scientific notation removes it.
questions.answer:
Written as 4500 g, it is unclear whether the trailing zeros are significant (i.e. measured to the nearest gram, giving 4 sig figs) or are placeholders only (measured to the nearest hundred grams, giving 2 sig figs).

Scientific notation removes the ambiguity because only the digits written in the coefficient are significant: 4.5 × 10³ g unambiguously shows 2 significant figures, while 4.500 × 10³ g unambiguously shows 4 significant figures.

questions.q: A chemistry lab report states: "The mass of the crucible was 24.10 g, measured to 4 significant figures." Explain whether this claim is correct, and identify how many significant figures the value 24.10 g actually has.
questions.answer:
The claim is incorrect. 24.10 g has 4 significant figures (2, 4, 1, 0), so in this particular case the stated count happens to be right for the wrong reason — but the general claim needs checking digit by digit:

Digits: 2 (non-zero, significant), 4 (non-zero, significant), 1 (non-zero, significant), 0 (trailing zero after the decimal point in a number containing a decimal point — significant). All 4 digits are significant, so 24.10 g does indeed have 4 significant figures; the report is correct.

questions.q:
State the number of significant figures in each of the following measurements.

(a) 0.03060 L

(b) 4500 mg (no decimal point given)

(c) 7.020 × 10³ s

(d) 90000 kg (no decimal point given)

(e) 0.000208 mol
questions.answer:
(a) 0.03060 L — 4 significant figures (leading zeros not significant; captive zero and trailing zero after the decimal point are significant: 3, 0, 6, 0).

(b) 4500 mg — 2 significant figures (no decimal point shown, so the trailing zeros are placeholders only: 4, 5).

(c) 7.020 × 10³ s — 4 significant figures (7, 0, 2, 0 — all digits in the coefficient are significant).

(d) 90000 kg — 1 significant figure (no decimal point; all trailing zeros are placeholders).

(e) 0.000208 mol — 3 significant figures (leading zeros not significant; captive zero and final digit are significant: 2, 0, 8).

questions.q:
Round off each of the following numbers to 3 significant figures.

(a) 82.457

(b) 0.0059826

(c) 128650

(d) 7.0049
questions.answer:
82.457 → 82.5 (3 s.f.; digit after cut - off is 5, round up)

0.0059826 → 0.00598 (3 s.f.; leading zeros not counted)

128650 → 129000 = 1.29 × 10⁵

7.0049 → 7.00 (3 s.f.; digit after cut - off is 4, stays the same)

questions.q: Three separate volumes of a NaOH solution, 14.2 mL, 3.554 mL and 0.08 mL, are combined. Calculate the total volume, giving your answer to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.answer:
Decimal places: 14.2 mL (1 d.p.), 3.554 mL (3 d.p.), 0.08 mL (2 d.p.). The least precise value has 1 decimal place, so the answer must be rounded to 1 decimal place.

14.2 + 3.554 + 0.08 = 17.834 mL

Total volume = 17.8 mL

questions.q: Calculate the following, giving your answer to the correct number of significant figures: 6.75 × 3.2 ÷ 0.150
questions.answer:
Significant figures: 6.75 (3 s.f.), 3.2 (2 s.f.), 0.150 (3 s.f.). The least precise value has 2 s.f., so the final answer must be rounded to 2 significant figures.

(6.75 × 3.2)/0.150 = 144.0

Answer = 140 = 1.4 × 10²

questions.q:
Convert each of the following numbers into correct scientific notation.

(a) 0.0003580

(b) 128900 (5 significant figures)

(c) 6.5

(d) 250000000 (2 significant figures)

Convert each of the following numbers from scientific notation back into standard (decimal) form.

(a) 4.02 × 10⁻³

(b) 7.1 × 10⁶

(c) 9.60 × 10⁻⁵
Perform the following calculation, giving your final answer in correct scientific notation: (2.5 × 10⁴) × (3.0 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (5.0 × 10²)
questions.answer:
( 2.5 × 10⁴ ) × ( 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ ) div ( 5.0 × 10² )

Multiply/divide the coefficients and add/subtract the exponents separately:

coefficient: (2.5 × 3.0)/5.0 = 1.5

exponent: 4 + ( - 6) - 2 = - 4

1.5 × 10⁻⁴

questions.q: One atomic mass unit (amu) is defined as 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. An atom of a certain isotope has a mass of 12.0 amu. Calculate the mass of this atom in kilograms, giving your answer in correct scientific notation.
questions.answer:
mass = 12.0 amu × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg

mass = 19.92 × 10⁻²⁷ kg

mass = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg (3 s.f.)

questions.q: A block of aluminium has a density of 2.70 g cm⁻³. Convert this density into kg m⁻³, showing your dimensional analysis clearly.
A gas cylinder has an internal pressure of 0.85 atm. Given that 1 atm = 760 mmHg (exact), calculate this pressure in mmHg to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.answer:
0.85 atm has 2 significant figures; 1 atm = 760 mmHg is an exact conversion factor, so it does not limit the significant figures of the answer.

0.85 atm × (760 mmHg)/(1 atm)

= 646 mmHg

Answer = 650 mmHg = 6.5 × 10² mmHg (2 s.f.)

questions.q: A pump delivers water at a rate of 3.2 L/min. Convert this flow rate into mL/s.
A chemical reaction produces a gas at a rate of 250 mg/s. Convert this rate into kg/hr.

Perform each of the following metric prefix conversions.

(a) 4.5 mg to g

(b) 250 μL to mL

(c) 0.0032 km to cm

(d) 78 ns to s

A student determines the density of an unknown metal sample experimentally as 8.35 g cm⁻³. The accepted (theoretical) density of the metal is 8.96 g cm⁻³. Calculate the percentage error of the student's result.

Two students, X and Y, each measure the boiling point of ethanol four times. The accepted (theoretical) value is 78.37 °C.

Student X (°C): 78.30, 78.35, 78.32, 78.31

Student Y (°C): 78.50, 77.90, 78.70, 78.10

(a) Calculate the average (experimental) boiling point recorded by each student.

(b) Calculate the percentage error for each student's average result.

(c) Using the range of each data set, determine which student's data is more precise, and explain how it is possible for both students to have a similar percentage error but very different precision.
questions.answer:
(a) Average boiling point:

avg X = (78.30 + 78.35 + 78.32 + 78.31)/4 = 78.32 circC

avg Y = (78.50 + 77.90 + 78.70 + 78.10)/4 = 78.30 circC

(b) Percentage error (theoretical value = 78.37 °C):

% error X = (|78.32 - 78.37|)/78.37 × 100% = 0.064%

% error Y = (|78.30 - 78.37|)/78.37 × 100% = 0.089%

(c) Range (a simple measure of spread):

range X = 78.35 - 78.30 = 0.05 circC

range Y = 78.70 - 77.90 = 0.80 circC

Student X's data has a much smaller range (0.05 °C vs 0.80 °C), so Student X's data is more precise. Both students have a similarly small percentage error because their averages happen to land close to the theoretical value, but Y's individual readings are scattered far more widely around that average — precision (reproducibility) and accuracy (closeness of the average to the true value) are independent properties of a data set, so a widely scattered set of data can still average out to an accurate result.

questions.q:
Round off each of the following calculations to the correct number of significant figures / decimal places:

(a) 12.5 × 0.020

(b) 100.0 ÷ 3.5

(c) 45.26 − 45.1

(d) 0.500 + 0.02 + 1.245

Carry out each calculation below, expressing the final answer in correct scientific notation:

(a) (6.02 × 10²³) × (2.0 × 10⁻³)

(b) (8.4 × 10⁵) ÷ (2.1 × 10²)

(c) (3.1 × 10⁻⁴) + (2.0 × 10⁻⁵)
A tray holding 4 identical samples of dried potassium hydroxide (KOH) has a total mass of 82.4 g. Calculate the mass of one sample, giving your answer to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.answer:
4 samples is an exact (counted) number, so it does not limit the significant figures of the answer; 82.4 g has 3 significant figures.

mass of one sample = (82.4 g)/4

mass of one sample = 20.6 g (3 s.f.)

questions.q:
Before a titration, a burette reads 2.40 mL; after the titration it reads 15.65 mL.

(a) Calculate the volume of titrant delivered, to the correct number of decimal places.

(b) State which digit in your answer is the uncertain (estimated) digit.
questions.answer:
volume delivered = 15.65 mL - 2.40 mL

volume delivered = 13.25 mL

(b) The uncertain (estimated) digit is the last digit, 5, in the hundredths place of 13.25 mL.

questions.q:
An unknown liquid has a mass of 45.60 g and occupies a volume of 36.8 cm³.

(a) Calculate the density of the liquid to the correct number of significant figures.

(b) Convert your answer to kg m⁻³.
questions.answer:
(a) Significant figures: 45.60 g (4 s.f.), 36.8 cm3 (3 s.f.) → answer to 3 s.f.

density = mass/volume = (45.60 g)/(36.8 cm³)

density = 1.24 g cm⁻³ (3 s.f.)

(b) Converting to kg m⁻³:

1.24 g/cm³ × 1000 = 1240 kg m⁻³ = 1.24 × 10³ kg m⁻³

questions.q: A carbon-12 atom has an actual mass of 1.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Given that 1 amu = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, calculate the mass of this atom in amu, and comment on whether your answer is consistent with the definition of the atomic mass scale.
questions.answer:
mass (amu) = (1.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg)/(1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg amu⁻¹)

mass (amu) = 12.0 amu (3 s.f.)

This is consistent with the atomic mass scale, since a carbon-12 atom is, by definition, assigned a mass of exactly 12 amu — the calculated value agrees with this defined reference point.

questions.q: A doctor prescribes a drug at a dose of 12 mg per kg of body weight for a 68 kg patient. The drug is supplied as a solution containing 250 mg per 5 mL. Using dimensional analysis, calculate the volume of solution (in mL) that must be administered, to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.answer:
dose = 12 mg/kg × 68 kg = 816 mg

volume = 816 mg × (5 mL)/(250 mg)

volume = 16.32 mL

Answer = 16 mL (2 s.f.)

questions.q:
A car travels at a constant speed of 95 km/h.

(a) Convert this speed to m/s.

(b) Convert this speed to cm/min.

Show your dimensional analysis for both parts and give each answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.answer:
(a) Converting km/h to m/s:

95 km/hr × (1000 m)/(1 km) × (1 hr)/(3600 s)

= (95 × 1000)/3600 m s⁻¹ = 26.4 m s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)

(b) Converting km/h to cm/min:

95 km/hr × (100000 cm)/(1 km) × (1 hr)/(60 min)

= (95 × 100000)/60 cm min⁻¹

= 1.58 × 10⁵ cm min⁻¹ (3 s.f.)
